hook.text: The Emancipation Proclamation freed slaves in 1863. Enslaved people in Texas didn't learn until 1865.

buildup.text: On June 19, 1865, Union soldiers arrived in Galveston, Texas, and announced the war—and slavery—were over.

discovery.text: Freed communities began celebrating the date immediately. It became the oldest African American holiday.

twist.text: Juneteenth wasn't a federal holiday until 2021—156 years after the event. Recognition came late.

climax.text: The gap between law and reality is the real lesson. Freedom on paper isn't freedom in life.

punchline.text: Liberation delayed is liberation's own story.

quiz.question: When did Juneteenth become a US federal holiday?

details.summary: Juneteenth (June 19, 1865) marks when enslaved people in Galveston, Texas — the last to learn of emancipation — finally received news of their freedom, two and a half years after the Emancipation Proclamation. It became a US federal holiday in 2021 after 156 years of grassroots celebration.
details.whyItMatters: Juneteenth's long journey from local Black celebration to federal holiday reflects America's slow, ongoing reckoning with slavery's legacy and the gap between legal freedom and actual equality.
takeaways: Juneteenth marks June 19, 1865 — when Texas slaves learned of freedom
The Emancipation Proclamation had been issued 2.5 years earlier
It became a US federal holiday in 2021

faq.question: Why did it take so long for enslaved Texans to learn of freedom?
faq.answer: The Emancipation Proclamation took effect January 1, 1863, but enforcement depended on Union military presence. Texas was remote from major battlefields, and slaveholders suppressed the news.

faq.question: Why did it take until 2021 to become a federal holiday?
faq.answer: Juneteenth was celebrated in Black communities since 1866 but was largely unknown to white America. Texas made it a state holiday in 1980. Activists campaigned for federal recognition for decades.
